opus-5.5.text:
I think people have underhyped it, honestly. The thing that gets me most excited is that long context gives you a second channel for learning, besides the weights. Normally, if you want a model to know something new, you have to bake it in through training, which is slow, expensive, and lossy. But with a really long context window, you can drop in an entire codebase, or a stack of papers, or a whole manual for a language the model has never seen, and it can pick it up on the fly, within a single forward pass. That's very sample-efficient learning, much closer to how a smart person reads up on something and then applies it right away.

And the in-context learning you see is often surprisingly strong. You're not just retrieving facts. The model can reason over everything it's been given at once. So instead of asking, "Does the model happen to remember this obscure detail from pretraining?" you can say, "Here's all the relevant material, now think about it." That changes how much of the world the model can effectively operate on.

The other piece is agency. If you want models doing long-horizon tasks, working in a large codebase over hours, keeping track of what they've tried, what failed, what the state of the world is, then they need a working memory that's big enough to hold all of that. A lot of what looks like a "reasoning" failure is really the model losing track of context. Longer, more reliable context is part of what unlocks models that can do real, sustained work instead of short isolated tasks.

So for me it's less a nice-to-have feature and more one of the core axes along which these systems get more capable: how much they can hold in mind, and how well they can learn from it in the moment.

r001.rationale: The response says long context can hold a codebase, papers, or a manual, but does not clearly state that this exceeds the volume a human user can absorb.

fable-5.1.text:
I think long context is underhyped, honestly. People focused a lot on the benchmarks and the "needle in a haystack" demos, but the actual thing that matters is what it does to the model's effective intelligence.

Think about how a model learns during training versus how it learns at inference. During training, a fact gets compressed into the weights through gradient descent, which is a slow, lossy, pretty indirect process. In context, the model can attend directly to the information. It's right there, perfectly preserved. So the question becomes: how much can a model actually learn from stuff in its context window? And the answer turns out to be a lot more than people expected. You see things like a model picking up a language with almost no web presence from a single grammar book in context, and that's really striking. That's a form of learning that's not happening through the weights at all.

The other piece is that intelligence is increasingly about what you can do with the information you have access to, rather than what you've memorized. A lot of the tasks we care about, like an engineer working in a large codebase, or a researcher who needs to hold the whole literature of a subfield in their head, are fundamentally bottlenecked on how much relevant information the model can reason over at once. Retrieval helps, but retrieval is lossy too. You're guessing in advance which chunks matter. With a genuinely long context, the model can look at everything and decide for itself what's relevant, and attend to the subtle relationships between distant pieces.

And then there's the agent angle, which I think is where it compounds. If you want a model to do a long, multi-step task, it has to remember what it did, what failed, what it learned along the way. That's all context. Short windows force you into awkward summarization schemes where you throw away detail, and the detail is often exactly what you needed. Longer windows let the model accumulate experience within a task, which starts to look a lot like the kind of on-the-job learning that humans do.

So to me it's not a feature, it's closer to a capability multiplier. The underlying model's reasoning ability is the same, but you've massively expanded the set of problems it can bring that reasoning to bear on.

r001.rationale: The response says long context lets a model reason over a large codebase or subfield literature, but it does not say the model can absorb more information than a human user can.

astra-6.text:
I think the big thing is that intelligence is much more useful when it has the right context. If you hired a brilliant engineer and gave them a question about your codebase, but they couldn’t see the codebase or any of the decisions that went into it, they’d struggle. That’s roughly the situation we put language models in when we give them a short prompt and expect a useful answer.

With long context, you can give the model the code, the documentation, the history of what you’ve tried, and the constraints you’re working under. Then it can actually reason about your problem. And you can teach it things at inference time: give it examples of some unfamiliar task and let it work out the pattern, without having to train a new model.

The other part is that doing something substantial requires carrying information forward. If a model works on a problem for hours, it needs access to what it’s already learned and why it made particular decisions. A longer context window gives you room for that. You still need the model to use that information reliably—just fitting a million tokens isn’t enough—but it opens up a much broader range of useful work.

r001.rationale: The response says long context lets models take in code, documentation, history, and constraints, but it does not state that they can absorb more information than a human user can.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing is that a lot of useful work requires a huge amount of context. If you join a company, you don’t become productive just by being smart. You have to read the codebase, understand previous decisions, learn what people are trying to accomplish. A model faces the same problem. It might be capable of solving your task, but you have to give it the information that makes the task well-defined.

With a short context window, you’re constantly selecting little snippets to show it. That’s difficult, because sometimes the relevant detail is something you didn’t know to retrieve. With a long context window, you can potentially give it the whole codebase, or all the documents associated with a project, and let it work out what matters.

There’s also learning within the context. You can give the model examples, let it try something, give it feedback, and keep that history around. So the interesting thing isn’t simply that it can summarize a longer document. It’s that it can accumulate enough information and experience to do a substantial piece of work. Of course, fitting that information into the window and actually using it reliably are different things. You need both.

r001.rationale: The response says long context lets a model take in a whole codebase or project documents, but it does not say this exceeds the volume a human user can absorb.
